content: Sodium peroxide, with the chemical formula Na₂O₂, is the typical product formed when sodium is burned. It is a potent oxidizing agent. Chemical Properties Sodium peroxide undergoes hydrolysis when it comes into contact with water, resulting in the formation of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). The hydrogen peroxide produced in this reaction rapidly decomposes in the resulting basic solution, yielding water (H₂O) and oxygen gas (O₂). This reaction is highly exothermic, meaning it releases a significant amount of heat, which can ignite combustible materials. Sodium peroxide is also highly reactive with many organic liquids, particularly alcohols and glycols, and can cause them to catch fire upon contact. Additionally, it reacts violently with powdered metals and numerous other compounds, often requiring only minimal initiation to trigger these reactions. When heated, sodium peroxide undergoes a structural phase transition at 512°C into a phase with unknown symmetry. Upon further heating beyond its melting point of 675°C, the compound decomposes, releasing oxygen gas (O₂) before it can reach a boiling point. Preparation Sodium peroxide can be synthesized by directly reacting sodium metal with oxygen gas at temperatures between 130°C and 200°C. Alternatively, it can be produced by passing ozone gas (O₃) over solid sodium iodide (NaI) within a platinum or palladium tube. In this process, the ozone oxidizes the sodium to form sodium peroxide, while iodine is released as iodine crystals, which can be sublimed with mild heating. The platinum or palladium acts as a catalyst for the reaction and remains unaffected by the sodium peroxide. Uses Due to its strong oxidizing properties, sodium peroxide is employed in the bleaching of wood pulp for paper production. It has also been utilized in the extraction of minerals from various ores. Commercially, sodium peroxide may be referred to by the trade names Solozone or Flocool. In chemical synthesis, it serves as an oxidative reagent in various preparative processes.
